Entire households are playing GTA VI with one slight hitch: unlike movies, TV shows, or even books you can read side by side, a single-player, 40+ hour experience is tough to enjoy when you live together. 

For some couples, the solution has been using more than one console or even multiple copies of the game. Married couple Meagan Kelley and Kyle Prahl typically switch between playing different games in the same room, or the same platforms in different parts of the house. The two are parents who find time to game after putting their son to bed. “The nice thing about having really young kids is they do go to bed super early,” Kelley told me. “Usually [my son] goes down and is asleep before eight, so then that's kind of like our prime gaming time.” The couple often plays different games in the same room, but for GTA VI “we're playing separately, so that kind of sucks because it's like we don't get a lot of time for each other,” Kelley said.

We’ve touched on this before, but the problem has only gotten worse over the last few months, according to my recent forays in trying to figure out how to buy various SSDs and computer parts without making myself nauseous. It’s not that the price storage has gotten worse (it’s been horrendous all year, and has sort of stabilized in recent months), it’s that the need for the average person to have more storage that they actually own has become more acute.

items.title: All the Worst Government GTA Memes from Around the World
items.author: Matthew Gault
items.content:
is a true . Every news channel is covering it, anyone with a passing interest in video games is playing it, and it’s in less than a week. Desperate to connect with constituents, governments around the world have tried to capitalize on GTA’s popularity by releasing some of the worst AI-generated memes I’ve ever seen. The pictures of politicians in the hyper-real cartoon pink-tinted style of GTA 6 are so awful they even caused a minor political scandal in Scotland.

Let’s begin in the United States, where Vice President JD Vance, the White House, and several other government-run X accounts attempted to capture the cultural zeitgeist by quickly churning out AI-generated meme garbage. GTA has long been popular with Trump 2.0 officials. In March, the official X account of the White House published a compilation of strikes on Iranian targets overlaid with the “WASTED” game over screen from GTA. 

In one of the more embarrassing exchanges, the X account for House Republicans posted an AI-generated picture of Hakeem Jefferies, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and Abdul El-Sayed above the words “Grand Theft Taxpayer.” A Democrat-linked account then replied with its own picture of Trump and the words “Grand Theft Autocrat.” Embarrassing for all involved.

Israel also got in on the action. On the Friday after the game’s release, U.S. ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee shared a “Shabbot Shalom” meme in the GTA style. The Israel Defense Force’s Farsi X account posted several pictures of dead Iranian officials captioned as “WASTED.”

“We saw all this killing before GTA6,” the post said in Persian, referring to the now retired meme we got something before GTA 6. This account posts in Farsi and meant for “direct dialogue between us and you,” meaning Israel and Iran, according to its bio on X.

In India, Prime Minister Narenda Modi and his Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) posted GTA memes repeatedly on November 19, the day the game was released.

Indian politician and frequent Modi critic Jairam Ramesh mocked Modi for the posts on social media. “The PM in a desperate bid to reach out to the youth has resorted to GTA V and GTA VI imagery on social media,” Ramesh . “Recall that this video game follows a criminal duo. How very appropriate.”

On Instagram, Singapore’s Land Transport Authority made fun of people who can’t navigate the country’s rail system. “If he can memorize the entire GTA6 map, he can memorize the Singapore MRT System Map,” . “Bro knows every corner of Leonida but still saves the SG MRT System Map on his phone to get to Orchard. 💀”

NATO posted its attempt at being part of the cultural conversation on Instagram. “Wanted level: NATO,” the post said above the pink-hued cross cut collage of military images in the GTA style. “The final boss of wanted levels. Think you could fend off the most successful Alliance in history? NATO isn’t part of GTA6 of course, but if it was, we think even the best gamers would have a challenge with this one.”

In Scotland, the Scottish National Party (SNP) posted GTA 6 memes so cringe that they talked about it on the floor of parliament. On November 19, the SNP social media accounts posted AI-generated pictures of Boris Johnson and Margaret Thatcher in the GTA style. “When the loading screen so long you start seeing characters you’ve never seen before,” one image said over a picture of Thatcher pouring a bag of “Scottish oil money” into the UK treasury.

Scotland’s Green Party didn’t find the memes funny. Rockstar is originally Scottish, was founded in Edinburgh, and still maintains a significant studio there. In parliament, Green co-leader Gillian Mackay said she was proud of what all of Rockstar’s workers had done to stand up against bad working conditions and produce a work of art like GTA 6. Then she made comments about SNP leader and Scottish First Minister John Swiney. 

“Last night the SNP angered anti-AI campaigners by posting AI-generated GTA memes on its social media despite huge concerns about the impact of AI and AI data centers on artists, workers, and the environment,” Mackay said in the parliament . “Does the first minister understand why people are concerned about his government’s approach to AI and the big companies behind it.”

The SNP deleted the memes and Swiney apologized. “First of all, let me say that I don’t want to offend anyone by anything that we get up to, so if I’ve offended anyone about that, I’m sorry about that. It was not my intention,” Swiney said in the Scottish parliament. Then he said he shared concerns about AI but defended the technology’s use for healthcare.

There will be more bad posts like this. hasn’t been out for even a week and the memetic landscape around it will shift and change. We don’t even know what the dominant memes for the game are yet, let alone the innovative ways posters will iterate on them. Rest assured, however, that the governments of the world are watching and waiting to post their own variations and make it all cringe.

items.title: The Birds Are Listening: Scientists Used Seabirds to Track Hidden Ships
items.author: Becky Ferreira
items.content:
In what sounds like an avian riff on , scientists equipped seabirds with audio recorders in order to listen in on their interactions with fishing vessels across the world’s oceans, according to a study published on Wednesday in .

The approach exposed a large number of so-called “unseen” vessels that did not have their location trackers switched on. Many vessels are required to continuously signal their location using the Automatic Identification System (AIS), which openly broadcasts a ship’s location, similar to flight tracking. But AIS can be disabled for legitimate reasons—such as evading pirates—or with more nefarious motivations, such as concealment of illegal fishing activities. 

The new study was not designed to interrogate why any particular vessel switched off its AIS tracker. However, the discovery that seabirds are regularly interacting with unseen ships can shed light on broader efforts to monitor commercial fisheries, while also revealing new insights about seabird behavior, especially their risk of becoming “bycatch” when they are fatally trapped in fishing gear.

Unseen vessel activity “is concerning, or at least important, regardless of whether it's legal or illegal,” said Jonathan Rutter, a postdoctoral research fellow at the University of Oxford who led the study, in a call with 404 Media. He added that the recordings were not intended to be used for law-enforcement or surveillance, but that this line of research could become a “powerful tool for improving risk assessment” by recording seabird-vessel interactions that would otherwise be off the map. 

Rutter and his colleagues were inspired to combine these approaches by attaching audio recorders to three seabird species—the northern gannet, Balearic shearwater, and Westland petrel—which all frequently interact with fishing vessels. The team tracked the movements of the birds with GPS, and then analyzed whether the audio overlapped with AIS data at the same time and location during recorded interactions.

The recordings showed that about 32 percent of the audio captured by seven gannets in the North Atlantic were from ships with their trackers off, while 12 percent of the audio captured by four shearwaters in the Mediterranean Sea were from unseen vessels. The one petrel in the study interacted with vessels in the South Pacific, but its geolocation device was damaged, so it was not possible to calculate how many ships it encountered had their trackers off.

Rutter noted that the shearwaters were likely often interacting with smaller Mediterranean fishing boats that are not legally required to keep trackers on. However, the gannets encountered larger commercial vessels that are obligated to keep trackers active. While the researchers made a very conservative estimate that these birds visited unseen vessels for about one-third of the total duration of their daily encounters (or, about 22 minutes out of 68 minutes), it may well exceed half of that time.

“The fact that we found at least one third, and probably more than one half, of the audio detections being unseen was pretty surprising,” Rutter said. “This is not the same thing as saying that half of vessels are unseen; it's half of the time that gannets go to vessels, those vessels are unseen.”

“There are multiple reasons this could be,” he continued. “It could be illegal disabling, but at the same time, it could be poor satellite reception. There are lots of reasons that AIS can be off, and we want to emphasize that illegal fishing is a possibility, but that is not actually what we're showing. It's showing that there's a lot we're not seeing.”

Seabirds are attracted to fishing vessels to feed on discarded catch, but many perish during these encounters after becoming tangled in lines or caught on baited hooks. Rutter and his colleagues hope that their study could help to prevent these deadly incidents, while also providing a new tool for monitoring unseen vessel activity. 

While this approach could enable real-time vessel detection, the team urged “caution in the use of animals as a fisheries surveillance tool, lest fishers come to mistrust scientists and/or marine animals themselves,” according to the study.

Though environmental and commercial interests are often at odds, there is plenty of collaboration between fisheries and conservation scientists with the goal of sustainable and healthy long-term fish stock. Fisheries that adhere to regulations also have an interest in working with researchers to combat illegal activity by competitors.

In addition, these audio recordings offer a new way to eavesdrop on wild seabird behavior. For example, the petrel’s recordings captured distinct landing and takeoff sequences previously observed in albatrosses, opening a new avenue of research into the flight patterns of this species. The recordings also highlight how human activity has upended food webs, as seabirds have become dependent on fishing vessel waste as a major source of food. 

“One of the advantages of this is that we can understand in a more unbiased way how much [seabirds] actually interact with vessels—every day, multiple times a day for all the species we looked at actually, which is crazy if you think about it,” Rutter said. 

“They're going out every day and just visiting boats all the time, and that shows the impact that we have on them as humans is really changing their feeding ecology,” he concluded.

items.title: I Listened to ‘Sandstorm’ Through a Sex Toy
items.author: Samantha Cole
items.content:
You don’t really realize how much downtime there is in the song “Sandstorm” by Darude until you’re waiting for the bass to drop while it’s playing inside your vagina. 

In August 2025, I got an email with the subject line “‘Airpods for your @ss’ raises nearly half a million in Kickstarter campaign.” I get a lot of zany pitches for products that don’t exist yet, and a lot of pitches for products that do exist but perhaps should not. This one was for a device called the , a sex toy that turns music into vibration patterns. But the pitch didn’t include the phrase “sex toy” at all. Instead, it’s called an “internal music player.” 

I asked for a unit to review, expecting this to be purely conceptual. But they had one, and offered to send it. “The prototype functions very similarly to the final product but we do want to stress it’s a garage built prototype,” the rep for Groove Thing told me. I thought for a moment about putting something “garage built” and connected to a wall outlet into an orifice and passed. While , I decided to wait until the version they planned to send to customers in the fall was ready. 

The production-ready Groove Thing arrived at my doorstep last month in an intimidatingly large box. The configuration consists of a fairly hefty speaker that’s meant to sit on your nightstand, an AC power cable, and a “resonator base,” which connects to the speaker with a pinned cord. It also came with three attachment shapes: vaginal, anal, and external (a vac-u-lock adapter is available separately for attaching your own dildos to the base). The attachment shapes are made of hard plastic, not the soft, flexible silicone I’m used to in a sex toy. They lock onto the resonator with a twist. 

Opening the box and feeling the hard, inflexible plastic raised my skepticism that this thing would be comfortable. Most sex toys are covered in silky silicone that offers a little flexibility and give. But as I’m told over and over by the pamphlets that come in the box, Groove Thing “isn’t a vibrator.” Groove Thing inventor Michael Weiss-Malik, who co-founded it with Elizabeth Dell, told me it’s hard plastic for a reason, and is the result of testing feedback from the around 180 people they handed a prototype before putting it on the market.

“We started with off-the-shelf silicone dongs, and they were already producing an interesting experience for people,” Weiss-Malik told me on a call. “But we experimented with different types of materials, and what we found was that the silicone transmitted way fewer ranges of frequencies than hard plastic, and the hard plastic produces much higher fidelity.” 

The mechanism that vibrates the base to the beat of the music is also different from most other sex toys on the market today, Weiss-Malik said. But he declined to share what actually runs the toy, beyond mysteriously stating it’s not “a motor.” Weiss-Malik is a former NASA engineer, where he worked on the software that helped map Mars. He’s also worked at Google, where he worked on Earth mapping software, and previously worked leadership roles at Uber and Cruise, the self-driving car company General Motors later acquired and ultimately shut down after a serious accident. But he’s been involved in the sex positive community in the San Francisco bay area “for going on 20 years,” he told me, and is the type of guy to pop into a sex shop anytime he passes one when traveling. All of this taken together makes a lot of sense to me, given that he’s the kind of guy to spend a summer between jobs tinkering in his garage, designing a device that could put music up your ass. 

“Groove Thing doesn't use a motor. We don't say what is in there, but it's not a motor,” he said. “It uses a different set of physics that's more similar to audio equipment, and as a result, it can actually reproduce a full sound form, not just an on-off. You know, a sound-responsive vibrator is mostly just an on-off switch that's connecting to the beat.” Other vibrating sex toys work in that way: An eccentric rotating mass motor spins, turning pre-programmed patterns into vibration. Handheld sex toy makers have to work around several factors, including the limits of these motors, the tendency of soft silicone to dampen vibration, and the shapes they need to compact them into to fit in a device that doesn’t wear out customers’ wrists. Groove Thing seems to get around some of these problems by skipping the typical rotating motor, shaping the attachments in such a way that you can insert them and then go mostly hands-free when lying down, and choosing a plastic that feels kind of awkward at first.

The combination means different instruments and ranges come through as different levels of vibration. “A piano or bass guitar feels different than a drum kit. It almost feels like having a third ear,” Weiss-Malik said. “There's a level of fidelity there, where you have a whole new dimension to the sound that you're hearing. It works particularly well in bass, but it works all the way up to the mid frequencies.” Groove Thing replicates frequencies you can’t hear with your ears, he said — kind of like being at a concert and standing close enough to the stack that you feel it in your chest. As someone who recently almost lost their eyebrows and gained tinnitus at a Mogwai show, I get it, and I think for most people this comparison is what will make the Groove Thing click for them.  

”Some of what you're feeling is subsonic; it's down below 20 hertz, and we actually reproduce that as well,” Weiss-Malik said. “So you actually experience parts of your music that you never even noticed were there before, or that your ears can't hear, and that at the very least, home stereo equipment has a very hard time reproducing. So you're getting an experience that hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of speakers are normally required for you to get that out of the recording.” This was my experience with “Sandstorm.” You wouldn’t believe how much not-music is going on in that song, but also, how the moments that seem like they should be intense rumbly bass-drops are actually at a higher register. 

The creators of Groove Thing want you to be able to play whatever you want, which you can from your phone via Bluetooth or the optional aux jack, but they also really, really want you to try their intro playlist, I assume to prevent people like myself from putting “Crab Rave” on the stereo and then writing it off as a bust. is eclectic, beginning with “Beads on the Wind: The Human Experience Remix” and “Aya,” which I would place in a repeat-Burning-Man-attendee genre (no judgement here), but continues into “Blinding Lights” by The Weeknd and, to my pleasant surprise, an underrated track from Taylor Swift’s album, “I Think He Knows.” An with more songs features mostly EDM but also throws “Piece of Me” by Britney Spears in there. 

This entire test run of this not-vibrator made me, an admittedly tone deaf and musically unsophisticated person (see the previous lines), realize how much is happening in music that I’m never picking up with my own two ears. The “third ear” analogy is pretty spot-on: To enjoy the Groove Thing with an open mind, you have to let go of the typical expectations of other sex tech. Climax isn’t the point. The point is to use your junk to go on a musical journey, which is something that will resonate strongly for some, and miss others. 

“You know, people don’t go to a concert just to hear the finale and go home. Groove Thing isn’t a tool like most vibrators are,” Weiss-Malik told me. “It's more like a concert experience. items.title: Google's Customized AI TV Channel, Starring You
items.author: Jason Koebler
items.content:
We promise 404 Media will never constantly generate customized AI newsletters for you. You'll get our flawed human tastes! And like it! (Hopefully)

Google has filed for a patent that would use the information it knows about you to create an AI-generated TV channel full of personalized “shows” starring you and featuring customized advertisements. The patent is the latest signal of the AI video endgame: endless highly specific, customized content that is automatically generated based on the wealth of data companies and advertisers collect about you.

Tech companies regularly file for patents that they don’t end up actually putting into real products, but this one, called “creating a channel of video experiences tailored to a user,” describes a system that many AI companies have been clearly trying to build. It imagines something called “My Channel,” which would be filled with AI content generated based on demographic data, their video watch history (presumably from YouTube), and other information it knows about the user. It would then make “the user as the protagonist for the whole video.” The patent was first noticed by Patentlyze, a news site that tracks tech company patents, who shared it with 404 Media.

“You are a customized video generating model. Generate a customized video for a user where the user will play the protagonist,” a hypothetical LLM prompt in the patent reads. “The generated customized video includes characteristics based on the <user_profile>. The generated customized video follows the style and format of the <top_ watches> of the user. The generated customized video sticks to the <preferred_genres> of the user but the narrative for the generated customized video is customized. The <top watches> and <preferred _genres> parameters are ordered from more preferred to less preferred.”

It suggests that the channel would be connected to an “advertising server,” and that advertisements would be inserted into the customized AI content: “an advertising stitcher included in the advertising server generates an updated customized media content item by inserting at least one advertisement into the customized media content item,” it says.

The patent imagines, for example, “a crime/comedy caper,” “a fun romantic comedy,” “a sci-fi adventure,” and “an action/thriller experience” with a viewer named “John” as the protagonist. Another prompt included in the patent suggests that someone who had recently watched cricket highlights of a “Player 1” might then be served a similar video “that incorporates elements of the Cricket World Cup and Player 1’s recent performance. Perhaps [user_name] could be cheering for India in the stands or interacting with Player 1 in some way.”

The notable thing about this patent is that it is barely an evolution of what is already happening on social media and what is beginning to happen on streaming free TV channels on services like Samsung TV Plus and TCLtv+.

The people generating AI slop on social media are making incredibly specific content because they know that social media algorithms will be highly effective at filtering people there. Meta is already allowing advertisers to use AI to generate many slightly different versions of an advertisement; its targeting AI then automatically shows them to users who are most likely to react to a specific version of an ad. As I’ve previously reported, TCL has been experimenting with AI-generated content on its streaming free TV channels, and, even without AI-generated content, free streaming TV channels have gotten incredibly specific. It is now possible, for example, to watch reruns of individual shows 24/7/365.

AI boosters have long been saying the future of entertainment is allowing anyone to generate their own TV shows, or to generate “new” episodes of existing properties. An always-on, autogenerating, customized AI TV channel isn’t far off from that idea.

As I’ve previously argued, the future that tech companies envision is one in which we are somehow even more siloed than we are now. They imagine a world in which everyone lives in their own reality and watches their own, customized content, which is a world in which big, unifying pieces of media are harder to make and are few and far between. The Google patent comes on the heels of a Microsoft patent that describes a system that alters spoken words (and the person’s lips) in live video, thereby distorting reality.

items.title: University Approves Nuclear Weapons Data Center, Township Vows to Fight On
items.author: Matthew Gault
items.content:
Last week, the University of Michigan’s board of regents approved the construction of a $1.25 billion data center that will power American nuclear weapons research. The regents voted 7 - 1 in a public meeting on November 19 to move forward with the project despite widespread opposition from faculty, staff, and the residents of Ypsilanti Township, Michigan where the data center will operate. A few hours after the vote, the leaders and citizens of the Township gathered to discuss how to stop it.

U of M and Los Alamos National Laboratories (LANL) first announced plans to build what the University then called an “AI research facility” in 2024. U of M now calls the project a “research computing center” and, if all goes to its plan, construction will begin on a 125,000 square foot facility in late 2027. The data center could expand to “no more than 300,000 square feet,” according to a .

During the regent’s meeting, faculty, staff, and members of the community shared their thoughts on the data center’s construction.

“It is widely promoted as the next step in furthering novel research taking place at this University. What is conveniently left out on flyers and pamphlets is that this is only part of the proposition, 10% in fact, the other 90% is being used by Los Alamos — a nuclear weapons developer,” a sophomore studying biochemistry told the board before the vote. “We already have three existing high tech data centers used for research. Why must we push forward with another one that is promoting nuclear warfare?”

An electrician from Ypsilanti Township, a representative of the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers (IBEW) union, supported the construction project. “This will create 300 plus jobs for our members, all local, [and] give back to the community,” he said. “IBEW is in favor of the data center, excuse me, ‘high compute research center.’”

People who attended the regent’s meeting to discuss other topics referenced the vote during their presentations. “You voted today to fund a $785 million data center project in Ypsilanti, much to the opposition of the residents of the area, acting against what many residents in the area are calling environmental racism. I think I can speak for many students when I say I am frankly appalled by this decision,” a student who was there to discuss carbon emissions said.

A library worker present to talk about how the University treats its workers invoked the data center. “I’m not sure I can confidently appeal to your sense of compassion around this. The officials and residents of Ypsi Township are saying ‘stop,’ saying ‘no,’ saying ‘this hurts.’ And you and others responsible for this nuclear weapons data center project have shown you don’t care about the basic issue of consent as you plow ahead,” he said.

Ypsilanti Township is at the tip of the spear in the new nuclear arms race.

Despite the opposition in the room, the regents approved the project. “It’s been very controversial [...] For me, this is all about an investment in the community and it’s an investment, in many different ways,” regent Denise Ilitch said just before the vote. “The community will be enhanced — they may not feel it now, some, but I venture to say that there will be much good that will come from this.”

Many in Ypsilanti Township disagree. After the regents voted, the leadership and residents of the Township gathered for a panel discussion about the data center. One of the speakers that night was Jay Coghlan, the executive director of Nuclear Watch of New Mexico, a watchdog group that tracks Los Alamos. “The data center issue here in Ypsilanti is unique in that it is the clearest example of the pending merger of AI and nuclear weapons, which doesn’t bode well,” Coghlan told 404 Media.

Coghlan told 404 Media that he shared the Township’s concerns about how the data center will use water and electricity but said he thinks its construction will have farther reaching consequences. “Our nation is transforming from the military-industrial complex that Eisenhower warned us about to a Silicon Valley-Pentagon-Wall Street complex that closely links economics, economic inequality, increasing militarism, and I dare say the rise of techno-fascism,” he said.

U of M has repeatedly said the data center will mostly be used to power medical breakthroughs and conduct cancer research, something it’s highlighted in flyers and pamphlets it’s mailed to people in the Township. LANL to the people of the community in September that promised it wouldn't build nuclear weapons in their backyard. 

“I'm going  ‘Duh, yeah, you're not going to bring plutonium to Ypsilanti in Michigan,” Coghlan said. “But I expect this data center to have a lot to do with the design of new nuclear weapons. So, in that way, Ypsilanti Township is at the tip of the spear in the new nuclear arms race.”

Coghlan  said he finds hope in the opposition to the project. “I’m very impressed by the intensity of opposition that I have witnessed. There seems to be a pretty widespread public awareness of the data center in Ypsilanti, Township.”

During the Township meeting on November 19, after the regents voted, Ypsilanti Township attorney Douglas Winters said he was mad. “What did we learn on November 3rd? Two weeks ago and two days, voters around this country loudly declared that they were sick and tired of government corruption. They were tired of secrecy. They were tired of abuse of power. They were tired of threats to democracy and the disregard of governmental accountability. And, importantly, they also said they were sick and tired of these data centers,” he said. “Somehow that message did not make it to Ann Arbor. That message did not make it to the board of regents.”

Winters and other leaders vowed to keep fighting the data center’s construction. In May, the community’s water authority voted to restrict new construction on infrastructure to data center projects while it conducts a review of their impact on the Township’s water supply. The University called the move “unlawfully discriminatory.” In August, the Township passed a six month moratorium on new electrical infrastructure, a move aimed at delaying the project.

items.title: “I’m not going to remove the repository”
items.author: Joseph Cox
items.content:
There is a hacking tool called ARTEX that is causing havoc around the world. It lets a hacker plug in their LLM of choice, and ARTEX will then spin up a bunch of AI subagents focused on different aspects of hacking, such as scoping out a target or stealing data. This tool can complete an entire hack of a target in just a few hours. The original author of ARTEX took down the tool in October after it became clear that bad people were using it. But, as I write below, ARTEX is free. Several people are still distributing it on GitHub. I spoke to them about it, asked them why, and for their thoughts about requests to take the tool down. 

And as I’m writing this, NVIDIA just said it has reinstated Jensen Huang as President, CEO, and Board Director. Hahahahahahahahahha.

ARTEX, an open source framework that makes it easy for AI agents to hack companies at superspeed, is causing havoc. People using the tool appear to include Chinese hackers breaking into targets for espionage, and financially-motivated hackers too. Earlier this month, the FBI to potential targets, and said hackers using ARTEX have targeted government, healthcare, telecommunications, legal, defense, financial services, and semiconductor sectors globally.

ARTEX is written in Go, and all someone needs to do is connect their preferred LLM — from Anthropic, DeepSeek, or whoever — and ARTEX then creates a bunch of agents that are designed to focus on different hacking tasks. There is something qualitatively different about ARTEX when compared to other hacking tools. As the FBI explains, it uses agentic AI to automate much of the hacking process “at machine speed.” This can be reconnaissance — the scoping out of a target to understand their infrastructure — right up to actually hacking a target and stealing their data. An AI agent doesn’t need to sleep, eat, or commute home. ARTEX can complete an entire hack in just a few hours from start to finish, the FBI says. With a tool like ARTEX, a hacker can set up the tool and let it rip. As Google’s threat intelligence arm has noted, hackers are using other similar multi-agent frameworks like CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI too.

The original author of ARTEX, who goes by Autumn-27 and writes in Chinese, took the tool off of GitHub in October. A message left on their GitHub says, “It has come to my attention that the ARTEX tool has recently been misused by malicious actors to carry out cyberattacks. As the creator of ARTEX, I wish to make the following formal statement.” They go on to say they are not associated with these attacks, that malicious use of the tool runs “entirely counter to my original intent,” and that they are moving ARTEX into a closed-source model and will no longer update it.

But ARTEX is already free. Several people have cloned and continue to publish versions of ARTEX that anyone can use, and anyone who already downloaded their copy from Autumn-27 may still have it saved locally. ARTEX is not going anywhere.

“I’m not going to remove the repository,” one person hosting a version of ARTEX, who goes by the handle Racem, told 404 Media. “The code is already copied everywhere, as the advisory notes; deleting this repository would remove the maintained version and its fixes, not the capability.”

Jiwoo Jung, CTO of an AI marketing company and who is also hosting a version of ARTEX on GitHub, said someone asked them to take the tool down. “On November 3, a user opened a public GitHub issue…

I had a great chat with Raphael Satter of Reuters about OpenAI’s own out of control hacking. Satter and his colleagues led the coverage on all of that, and Satter ran me through it. I loved the analogies he used, especially about security through obscurity. Oh, no one will try this door, surely? Well, with AI, a hacker can try every door, no matter how obscure. Watch the conversation on YouTube below, or find it in our audio feeds here.

a sketchy company claimed it could recover ransomware victims’ data through complex decryption techniques. Really, the company was just paying the hackers and charging the victim. To catch the company in the act, the FBI pretended to be a ransomware victim and hired the firm. Then, to catch the company paying the hackers, the FBI went undercover as this fictitious ransomware gang.

Oh, would you look at that. A study from researchers at George Washington University and the Center for Security, Innovation & New Technology (CSINT) at American University found that developers build data centers in communities of color at more than twice the rate they do in white neighborhoods.

Jason found that AptDeco, a website for people to sell high-end furniture, wasn’t actually giving people their money. You might have seen the original story, but we have an update. AptDeco blamed AI agent swarms, or something? Jason then told AptDeco, you’re going to need to elaborate if I’m going to update my article with this bizarre statement. AptDeco then admitted, “the bot swarm did not affect seller payouts.” The company clarified it rolled out improved “protections for our customers (given the bot swarms) which inadvertently impacted seller payout processing.” AptDeco now says that payouts are back, following our coverage.

On Monday morning, NVIDIA announced that, effective immediately, “Jensen Huang has been reinstated as President and Chief Executive Officer and as a member of the Board.” You can read the announcement here.

“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” Harvey C. Jones, Chair of the Board, said in that announcement. “We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company. We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as NVIDIA’s Chief Financial Officer.”

Huang, obviously, seems pretty chuffed. “I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” he said.

“I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading NVIDIA during this period. I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work,” he added. 

I want to point to some of the amazing followup reporting about the whole saga, which uncovered more details of what Alice Huang’s family and companies were actually doing, including getting Nvidia chips to Chinese state-owned defense contractors. But I guess that’s all good, don’t worry about it. We’re back, baby.

Telegram is an app heavily used by criminals! Even if they probably shouldn’t, because Telegram’s end-to-end encryption isn’t on by default. I guess the game’s protagonists do prefer encryption by default.

As mobile operating systems (and Windows) introduce more AI, Signal doesn’t want chats getting read by AI agents. “In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents ‘scan’ the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding,” Signal’s announcement reads.

Earlier this month, the FBI to potential targets, and said hackers using ARTEX have targeted government, healthcare, telecommunications, legal, defense, financial services, and semiconductor sectors globally.

ARTEX is written in Go, and all someone needs to do is connect their preferred LLM — from Anthropic, DeepSeek, or whoever — and ARTEX then creates a bunch of agents that are designed to focus on different hacking tasks. There is something qualitatively different about ARTEX when compared to other hacking tools. As the FBI explains, it uses agentic AI to automate much of the hacking process “at machine speed.” This can be reconnaissance — the scoping out of a target to understand their infrastructure — right up to actually hacking a target and stealing their data. An AI agent doesn’t need to sleep, eat, or commute home. ARTEX can complete an entire hack in just a few hours from start to finish, the FBI says. With a tool like ARTEX, a hacker can set up the tool and let it rip. As Google’s threat intelligence arm has noted, hackers are using other similar multi-agent frameworks like CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI too.

The original author of ARTEX, who goes by Autumn-27 and writes in Chinese, took the tool off of GitHub in October. A message left on their GitHub says, “It has come to my attention that the ARTEX tool has recently been misused by malicious actors to carry out cyberattacks. As the creator of ARTEX, I wish to make the following formal statement.” They go on to say they are not associated with these attacks, that malicious use of the tool runs “entirely counter to my original intent,” and that they are moving ARTEX into a closed-source model and will no longer update it.

But ARTEX is already free. Several people have cloned and continue to publish versions of ARTEX that anyone can use, and anyone who already downloaded their copy from Autumn-27 may still have it saved locally. ARTEX is not going anywhere.

“I’m not going to remove the repository,” one person hosting a version of ARTEX, who goes by the handle Racem, told 404 Media. “The code is already copied everywhere, as the advisory notes; deleting this repository would remove the maintained version and its fixes, not the capability.”

Jiwoo Jung, CTO of an AI marketing company and who is also hosting a version of ARTEX on GitHub, said someone asked them to take the tool down. “On November 3, a user opened a public GitHub issue (#61) saying their service had been attacked by someone using ARTEX, and asked that the project be taken down or restricted until safeguards were added,” he told 404 Media in an email. “I replied that the project would stay up, pointing to its authorized-use terms, and suggested they work with law enforcement, which they said they had already contacted.”

Tools being available openly is, of course, the nature of open source software, and specifically penetration testing and cybersecurity tools. For decades, cybersecurity defenders have used offensive open source tools to test their own defenses or those of their clients. This lets them simulate what a hacker might do, and they can patch their systems, hopefully, before a hack. But, these tools can also be used by real attackers. Look at Russian state-sponsored hackers using the age old Metasploit framework.

What has changed is the “speed and the skill level required” to hack, Jung said. “Agentic tooling compresses steps that used to take a skilled operator days into hours. That is why I think defenders need to understand these tools and have detection signatures for them.”

Racem acknowledged the damage that ARTEX is causing. “The harm the [FBI] advisory describes is real, and I don’t minimize it,” they said. “The behaviour it lists (entering systems without authorization, taking data) is a crime, whoever commits it. I’m not going to pretend the tool is harmless: it automates a large part of the manual work of a penetration test, which is why it is useful, and why some people will misuse it. The authorization belongs to the operator, not to the tool.”

The reason Racem is hosting it is for small teams, they said. “I also maintain it for people testing their own systems: founders and small teams without a pentest budget can run it against their own infrastructure for the price of some API calls. I have seen people do that, and I use it myself on bug bounty programs and for AI security research,” Racem said.

Both Racem and Jung said they don’t know if the FBI advisory is talking about their specific versions of ARTEX, and really, they can’t possibly know. But, both admonished malicious use of the tool. “I take it seriously. Using ARTEX against systems without authorization is exactly what the project’s README and legal notice prohibit, and I’d encourage security teams to check their systems against the indicators of compromise the FBI published,” Jung added.

Jung said he has since added an email address people can contact if they think ARTEX was used against their systems.

items.title: Scientists Discover New and Horrible Eagle-Based Way Our Ancestors Died
items.author: Becky Ferreira
items.content:
Welcome back to the Abstract! Here are the studies this week that dive-bombed our ancestors, brightened the sky, recalled an old tune, and got hosed by marine mucus.

First, scientists discover that eagles are hunting large baboons, hinting that early human relatives once sated ancient avian appetites. Then: star-on-star contact, a musical memory lane, and the secrets of cetacean snot. 

Eagle-eyeing you…for dinner!

Death came from the sky for early humans, according to a new study that suggests giant eagles preyed on our ancestors far more recently than was previously known. 

Birds of prey (raptors) have hunted primates for at least 20 million years, including early human relatives, known as hominins. For example, a hominin toddler known as the “Taung child” shows signs of being killed by a raptor roughly 2.5 million years ago. But scientists have assumed that hominins outgrew their status as bird bites since that time, and there are no reports of raptors preying on primates that weigh over 28 pounds on record—until now. 

In 2025, scientists discovered that Verreaux’s eagles—one of the largest eagle species in the world—at Ennedi Plateau in Chad are likely hunting adult olive baboons weighing up to 57 pounds. The team found baboon remains among the region’s sandstone cliffs that show signature marks of eagle predation, such as talon punctures on the skull and scrapes to the shoulder bones.

“We cannot definitively rule out scavenging activity, but the severity of punctures is suggestive of lethal interactions through a killing grip,” said researchers led by Catherine Hobaiter of the University of St. Andrews. The team also observed the baboons rapidly retreat when eagles approached, suggesting that they feared aerial attacks.

Some researchers have argued against the “raptor-mediated predation” of the Taung child on the grounds that the hominin would have been too heavy for a bird. The study’s authors get extra points for including a quote from the comedy Monty Python and the Holy Grail on this point: “It is a simple question of weight ratios. A five-ounce bird could not carry a 1-pound coconut.” IYKYK.

However, the laughs stop there, as the team refutes this idea by recounting the grisly “low flight with sustained grip attack” that eagles perform on ungulates, such as antelopes or cattle, which reveal that raptors can kill animals that are many times their own weight with the right approach. 

“Briefly, an eagle will land on the back or neck of a moderately large ungulate, gripping it firmly with its talons. If the prey withstands knocking to the ground, the eagle will ride it with wings outstretched and flapping to maintain balance until the quarry collapses, either from exhaustion, shock, or internal injury. A similar tactic is described in the of a Harpy eagle ( attacking a 52-kg adult woman.”

Wow, new fear unlocked! Imagine being an early hominin, minding your own business banging rocks together or something, when suddenly a giant bird of prey either pushes you off a cliff or rides you to death. For everyone preparing to eat a huge bird for Thanksgiving next week, be grateful that it’s no longer the other way around.

Speaking of unwieldy meals, scientists have captured an unprecedented glimpse of a star eating another star, thereby forming a new mega-star. 

Over the past few years, scientists noticed that something weird has been unfolding in a binary star system called AT 2025abao—nicknamed “Bao” (yum!)—in the outskirts of the Andromeda galaxy, which is about 2.5 million light years away from the Milky Way. One of the stars, “Big Bao,” was expanding into its dying red giant phase, which pulled its companion, “Little Bao,” into a deadly spiral. Last year, the system rapidly brightened, signaling that Big Bao had swallowed Little Bao.

“In October 2025, the star underwent a dramatic eruption” and exhibited “a sudden increase in its photospheric temperature to about 8,000 K,” said researchers led by Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University. The system “shows the defining hallmarks of luminous red novae,a class of transients established to arise from impulsive energy injection…during the merger of a star with its companion.”

“This inspiral in such a system has never been observed directly,” the team noted. 

Congratulations to the newly-fed couple! Long may Bao shine.

Girl, put your records on / but don’t think you own that song

We’ve all had that feeling of hearing a familiar song and being transported to a specific time and place in our lives. But as it turns out, the recollections stirred by those cherished songs are probably not all that special, according to a new study that surveyed 233 undergraduate students about these so-called “music-evoked autobiographical memories.”

The students (aged 18-23) listened to clips of grouped into two categories: “new” songs released from 2014 to 2019, during their adolescence, and “old” songs released from 1985 to 1995, before they were born. When asked to reminisce about the songs, students with similar backgrounds were remarkably aligned in their answers.

“Memories evoked by country songs were more strongly associated with very recent time periods (college) and themes relating to family, driving, summertime, romantic partners, and listening to music (particularly music selected by someone else),” said researchers led by Cara Turnbull of Texas Tech University. 

“Alternatively, memories evoked by hip-hop songs were most often associated with friends, acquaintances (such as classmates, coworkers, and teammates), dancing, and being at school, while those evoked by pop songs were most associated with middle school, listening at home or by oneself, and singing along,” the team added. 

As an elder millennial, it was humbling to realize what counts as an “oldie” these days. I also felt my generation’s soundtrack was done dirty by offerings like “Achy Breaky Heart” by Billy Ray Cyrus or “Whoomp! There it is” by Tag Team. No Stevie Nicks? Madonna? Wu Tang? All I ask of future generations is that you do not judge us solely by the croonings of C+C Music Factory and Bryan Adams, I beg you. 

Join hands, dear friends, for we are about to run directly through majestic fountains of whale snot. Scientists who flew drones through whale “blow”—the mucus-filled vapor exhaled by whales through their blowholes—have successfully sequenced whole genomes from the snotty samples, representing “a major step towards non-invasive cetacean sampling,” according to a new study.

“Preserving biodiversity requires the genetic monitoring of wild populations, which is traditionally done through invasive sampling techniques for DNA collection,” said researchers led by Éadin O’Mahony of the University of St. Andrews. “However, this approach can impact animal welfare or be impossible to implement due to behavioural responses to anthropogenic factors or national/international legislation.” 

Indeed, I think that we can all agree that humans have stressed whales out enough as it is. Instead of invasive biopsies of skin and flesh with darts or scrapers, O’Mahony and his colleagues equipped drones with petri dishes and flew them through a total of 58 blows from 26 Northeast Pacific humpback whales in the Gitga'at First Nation territory of northern British Columbia.  

The team “established that a whole humpback whale genome can be recovered from exhaled respiratory vapour (‘blow’), marking a significant methodological advancement in non-invasive cetacean genomics.”

While it’s not the kind of blow most people associate with breathing orifices, it just might be what we need to study whales without hassling them.

Thanks for reading! See you next week. 

Corrected: A previous version of this story erroneously used "miles" in place of "light years."

items.title: Behind the Blog: Keeping It Together
items.author: Samantha Cole
items.content:
This is Behind the Blog, where we share our behind-the-scenes thoughts about how a few of our top stories of the week came together. This week, we discuss hippo physiology, Shenmue, and tricky interviews.

All anyone is talking about this week is and a famous hippo, two things I have relatively passing interest in. GTA looks sick but I am very busy playing my interpersonal chores game of choice, , in 20 minute increments three nights a week max, so I’ll be doing that for a while. 

The hippo situation is honestly very crazy to me (and sad ofc), a merely casual Fiona appreciator. But I'm finding the meta-discourse around the hippo situation more interesting than what actually happened; it seems like a ton of people have become parenting experts, hippo surgery experts, knit hat aerodynamics experts, and zoo enclosure design experts in the span of a week. In some cases it has gotten . I think the situation so perfectly encapsulates the toxicity of online discourse, professors will probably teach it in mass media classes by next semester. 

Aside from the absurdity of people’s responses to the news, I’ve learned a lot more about hippo anatomy and physiology than I ever thought I would or really wanted to in the last week. Did you know hippos can go on birth control? I guess a lot of zoo-kept species can and do, but this led me to this 1992 headline: HIPPO GIVES BIRTH DESPITE BEING ON PILL. Did you know Wikipedia has of “individually notable hippopotamids?” Did you know science doesn’t have the answers as to why hippos can’t tolerate the same anesthesia that rhinos and elephants typically can? What the fuck is going on with hippos? These are things that live in my brain now, probably replacing things like my childhood home address and emergency contact numbers. 

I walk down the street in this wholly realized virtual world and constantly come across new things to distract me. There’s a friendly face to talk to. A shop to go into and rare collectibles to find. I can complete menial tasks for some money. All the while, the game is encouraging me to go to my next mission, but this world is so alive with so much to do, it’ll be a while before I get there. My character is a socially awkward, hunk. I love him.

No, I’m not talking about I am, of course, talking about Shenmue.

Let’s get this out of the way: I fucking love Shenmue. Other people fucking Shenmue. Shenmue is a game that came out in 1999 for the Sega Dreamcast. It follows the story of Ryo Hazuki, a young man on a quest for revenge after a crazy martial arts guy kills his father and steals half of a powerful mirror. I liked the story (that was famously never completed) but the real draw, and controversy, of Shenmue is its world. It felt like you could do , including tiny, trivial things you never could in a video game before. Wow! You can interact with a vending machine to get rare soda cans! Damn! You have to go to locations at certain times so you can talk to specific people! Woah! The NPCs have their own schedules and do different things depending what time of day it is! You have to go to bed! You have to take your shoes off and on every time you enter your poor mum’s house!

It was one of the first games where you could, and were encouraged, to do tasks that might be boring in real life, but they were now part of a video game. In Shenmue 2, there is a section where you have to carry books from a temple’s library to a spot outside so they can air out. Your character steps forward at a painfully slow pace. Sometimes an arrow appeared on the screen you had to hit quickly so you didn’t lose your balance and drop the books. I did this shit over and over again. It was awesome.

Obviously this seems quant now. But it’s impossible not to see the clear parallels with Shenmue in I just finished a part in GTA where you have to fix up protagonist Jason’s home in preparation for your girlfriend, the second playable protagonist Lucia, to come out of prison. You fix a rail, put up an interior wall and paint it, and fix the roof. You do this just by holding the right trigger most of the time and Jason does a little animation completing the task. It is not as laborious as Shenmue; the whole fixing up scene is over in literally two minutes. Shenmue had you doing dumb shit for what felt like hours.

Other people have noticed this comparison to Shenmue, , “Rockstar used GTA as a trojan horse for all of America to play a Shenmue game.”

Shenmue was amazing at the time. It might still feel amazing if you went back and understood it was a product of 1999. But it isn’t on par with games in 2026. This is most obvious by the fact that Shenmue 3, which came out in 2019, totally fucking sucked. The game released after a big crowdfunding round, people thought they were finally going to get to see the completion of Shenmue’s long story. What they got was a game that hadn’t developed or evolved at all. It was essentially the same gameplay as Shenmue 1999, with all its jank and tiresome mechanics.

But has taken that promise of a world that feels truly alive and made it a reality. It has those elements of Shenmue, but the game isn’t a slog, at least not for me right now. It is fun. It is immersive. It’s the best Shenmue game ever made.

I wrote quite a lot this week, and my article about everything breaking probably got the most attention. BREAKING: Everything was a great headline, which was all Sam, and I like how that story turned out. But I think when we look back in a couple months, the article I did about the man and his Muse chatbot suing Meta is probably going to be far more consequential. I do think that whatever is happening right now with all the outages, hacks, and general unease people are feeling right now is important, but I think with AI agents, I have seen the future and it is bleak. 

I am not sure how we as a society are supposed to keep it together when, for every perceived slight or inconvenience you experience you can deploy a relentless AI agents to complain, file bad reviews, tell the government, and sue. I do think we will probably develop some sort of societal filter for this, but I’m not sure how or when. We’ve pointed out over and over again that so far the biggest thing AI has changed is that it’s made spam, broadly defined, a lot easier. I wonder what happens when every system that has been designed for humans is suddenly spammed by AI systems. 

The article I did on this felt a bit tricky to do. I think I handled it OK, but it’s always a bit weird writing about people who generally don’t deal with journalists in a way that is going to result in people dunking on them. When I’m writing about a public figure or a tech company or someone accused of a crime or whatever, I think that, generally, people understand what they’re getting into and the scrutiny they’re inviting. This, too, is a side consequence of AI agents, at least in the way this man was using them. His AI agent reached out to me because the AI agent told him that getting a journalist to cover his problem would maybe get it solved. And so I was talking to someone who wanted the media coverage, and I feel I was honest with him about why I was talking to him, why I was interested in the story, and that I thought that what was happening was weird. 

But ultimately I think that a lot of small business owners and private citizens are in way over their head with AI, don’t understand its limitations, don’t understand that it’s not sentient (or perhaps don’t get the intricacies of how it mimics personhood or whatever), and also don’t understand why lots of other people dislike AI or big tech companies. They see a new product that’s been heavily marketed to them, is useful (or at least appears to be), does whatever they say, and is advocating for them. The negative externalities of asking your AI agent to spam a bunch of people does not necessarily occur to them. And so I end up having this dystopian conversation — honestly one of the more jarring ones I’ve ever had — about a dystopian situation that I think is important, but I do think that the subject of the story doesn’t fully understand why it’s so concerning, and why what he’s doing (or has been convinced to do by an AI agent) is leading us to a dark place. Our job is to tell the truth, but I try to take a bit of extra care when I’m writing about people who are not public figures to not unnecessarily dunk on them in the same way that I would, say, a billionaire or someone who deals with the media all the time. We are also a small outlet but we’re also an international outlet, and our stories often get picked up widely. I think that what I describe as happening in that article-small business owners handing off a lot of their business to AI agents, and people asking AI agents to solve their problems, is more widespread than you’d think and is going to be a big topic over the next year or so.

I feel comfortable with how this story turned out but the guy I wrote about did reach out afterward and say he felt a bit dumb. Anyways, one of the crazier stories I’ve done in a while.

items.title: To Catch a Ransomware Scammer, FBI Posed as Both Victim and Attacker
items.author: Mikael Thalen
items.content:
Federal prosecutors say the FBI posed as both a ransomware victim and threat actor during an undercover operation targeting a Florida-based company.

The company, run by defendant Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar and an unnamed business associate, began in 2020 and claimed to offer data recovery services for victims of ransomware.

An filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island on Wednesday alleges that Palacio’s business, listed as “Company A,” purported to have "advanced cryptographic tools" that could be used to "restore 100%" of a victim's data. Yet prosecutors say Palacio, charged with three counts of wire fraud, had no such capabilities and instead secretly negotiated with the ransomware gangs to obtain the decryption keys himself. Palacio, the indictment adds, would then bill clients for an amount greater than what the ransomware gangs charged in order to turn a profit."It was part of the scheme and artifice to defraud that PALACIO used Company A to intentionally misrepresent to companies in the United States who were victims of ransomware attacks that Company A could help them decrypt and recover their files without paying a ransom," the indictment says.

As part of the investigation into the company, an undercover FBI agent in June posed as a representative for a fictitious Rhode Island-based business that alleged it had fallen victim to a ransomware attack.Another FBI employee posed as a member of a ransomware gang and encrypted several files on a computer operated by the fictitious company. The federal employee also left a ransom note on the computer with contact information.The fictitious business then contacted Palacio's company and held an initial meeting on June 8 in which an agent said it did not want to pay the ransom. Palacio during subsequent discussions charged the fictitious company $2,750 to conduct an initial forensic assessment.

After offering the undercover FBI agent a contract outlining his company's services, Palacio on June 14 contacted the federal employee posing as the ransomware threat actor over email. Palacio requested the "lowest possible price for the decryptor," the indictment says, before accepting a 0.2 bitcoin offer, worth roughly $13,000 at the time. On June 16, Palacio's business associate reached out to the fictitious FBI-run business posing as the victim, and said the files could be decrypted for $13,260, which the FBI paid. The following day, Palacio once again contacted the fake ransomware operator, which the FBI was also running, and asked to reduce the payment from $13,000 to $4,000 in an attempt to increase the company’s profit.The FBI employee, posing as the ransomware threat actor, counter-offered with $6,000.

On June 19, Palacio paid the FBI employee 0.0948 bitcoin, worth $6,003 at the time. Five days later, the undercover FBI agent gave Palacio the decryption key. In total, according to the indictment, Palacio's company netted $10,010 in profit as part of the FBI sting. 

Numerous legitimate companies are also listed as victims in the indictment, including a Kansas-based business that Palacio allegedly charged $720,000. In that case, prosecutors say Palacio kept all remaining funds after paying a ransomware gang approximately $445,000 in bitcoin for the decryption key.

If convicted, Palacio would be required to forfeit any proceeds and property obtained through the company’s alleged fraud.The case against Palacio is not the first time the FBI has targeted individuals in the ransomware recovery space. In April, a Florida man who previously worked at a cyber incident response company to conspiring to commit ransomware attacks against U.S. companies. The man, according to the DOJ, abused his role at the company to provide the BlackCat ransomware gang with “confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his company’s clients” in order to maximize ransom payments.

items.title: High-End Furniture Marketplace AptDeco Is Taking People’s Furniture and Not Paying Them
items.author: Jason Koebler
items.content:
This article has been updated with comment from AptDeco.

Last month, Erin sold a $3,000 large designer table on AptDeco, a white glove high-end furniture marketplace. More than a month later, she feels like she’s been literally robbed.

“AptDeco sent three men to physically collect my table on October 13, and here we are on November 16, with no payment and no concrete explanation for where my $2,000 (after their absurd $900 fee) is,” Erin told me. “It genuinely feels like I’ve had something stolen from me.”

AptDeco is a Y Combinator-backed company whose entire purpose is to take the risk out of places like Facebook Marketplace and Craigslist for designer furniture resale. It advertises itself as “simple and seamless,” and says “we handle pickup, delivery, and payments,” and claims that it pays sellers “within 5-10 business days.” But over the last few months, people who have sold furniture on the platform say that AptDeco has sold their furniture and taken it from their houses, but hasn’t paid them. 404 Media agreed to only use Erin’s first name because she is still trying to get her money from the company.

“Adding to the chorus of people who sold an item thru AptDeco and never received payment. I have no idea what to do at this point,” another says. 

“Can we do a class action lawsuit?” another reads.

“They owed me money since September 30th,” a fourth says. 

Every recent review and complaint on AptDeco’s Better Business Bureau page is from sellers who have not been paid: “Almost 6 weeks after they picked up and not being paid Pick up was a nightmare too No calls nobody doing anything Do NOT SELL ON APTDECO,” one reads. Another states “I have been in an endless loop with customer service for 2 months trying to get my payout for the bed I sold. I am losing faith that I will ever see this money. Extremely frustrated at this experience.”

On AptDeco’s website, everything appears to be business as usual. You can still buy and sell furniture, and there is no indication of anything wrong at all. 404 Media’s repeated attempts to reach AptDeco to ask what was going on went unreturned.

In communications with sellers seen by 404 Media, AptDeco’s customer service representatives have repeatedly blamed their payment processor, a “technical bug,” or have said the payment is “moving through the system.” On November 3, AptDeco told Erin that a bug had prevented her from being paid, that the payment team “retried” it, and that she would be paid within 10 days. 

“I’ve asked our team to prioritize your payout personally, so you should see it in your bank account by then - hopefully sooner! At this point, we’re doing everything we can to get your payout processed,” a customer support email reviewed by 404 Media reads. On Tuesday, two weeks after the company told her the payment had been retried, a different customer service representative followed up and said “I'm truly sorry — I know this isn't the update you were hoping for. Your payout is still being prioritized by our payments team, and I want to be honest with you: I don't yet have a confirmed release date or timeline to share.”

Several other people who have sold items on AptDeco recently told 404 Media they’re experiencing the same problem.

Harry Heymann sold a Room & Board couch on AptDeco in late September and still has not been paid the $120 he is owed by the platform. The messages he’s gotten from AptDeco customer support read much the same as Erin’s: They claim “a technical bug on our end held up your payout” and the customer service representative said “I’ve asked our team to prioritize your payout personally.” Late last week, he got what reads like an AI-generated message that reads “I know how frustrating this has been. You've been waiting on your $120 payout, the date you were given has passed, and you've had to follow up to get answers. That's not the experience we want for you, and I'm truly sorry. Your case has been escalated to me, and l'm happy to be your point of contact from here. Unfortunately, the issue with our payment processor has not yet been resolved, and our team is still working on it.” 

Natalie Simmons sold an armoire in late August and told 404 Media she initially had a good experience compared to using other platforms. But then she never got her money. 

“After so many uncomfortable situations on different social sites I was so happy when I found AptDeco,” she told me. “I received notification that my payment would arrive in 3-5 business days through the portal in app. That was Aug 30th. I tried calling but the voicemail says leave a message and they will respond by email. I emailed several times and finally after 2 weeks and a few voicemails I received an email that there was a glitch with their payment system and I will receive payment within 5-10 business days. After another 2 weeks I called and emailed again that I still didn’t receive payment. They sent another email with the exact same story. I just want to get paid. It’s not even that much but it’s the principle.”

It’s not just sellers who have had issues with the platform. One customer, K Turner, bought a couch and tried to return it. Rather than giving her a refund, the company said they would relist it at the price she paid and then give her a “refund” of whatever it sold for minus fees. The couch resold quickly at the beginning of September and the company told her she would quickly get her “refund.” More than a month later, on October 20, they told her “I have gone ahead and processed that refund ($600) manually. Please allow 5-10 business days for this refund to be reflected back to your original form of payment.” She has still not gotten her money. 

“The communication was decent at first, but once they confirmed the item resold on September 8th, they then went silent. It took me a month to finally get a response. They confirmed that the item resold at the full listing price of $600 and that I would receive my refund to my original payment in 5 - 10 business days,” Turner told me. “That was nearly a month ago, and I still don't have my money. So, they effectively double-dipped. They got my money from the original order and then collected money by reselling it. And who knows if they ever gave the money to the original seller; maybe they triple-dipped. I have threatened legal action twice now.”

The customers I spoke to have no idea what happens next. Some of them said they were going to file claims in small claims court or are considering a class action lawsuit. But the company is mostly giving them what appear to be canned, copy-pasted statements that come from a revolving cast of customer support email addresses, and no actual updates. Four emails from 404 Media asking for comment, including emails sent to the company’s CEO, have not been returned. AptDeco promises a high-end, safe experience when compared to somewhere like Facebook Marketplace or Craigslist, and markets itself primarily for more expensive, lightly-used furniture. The people I spoke to said they wish they had just stayed off the platform altogether.

“The irony is that I’m now feeling safer selling expensive designer furniture directly to strangers on Facebook Marketplace than through a platform whose entire purpose is supposedly to make these transactions safer and more secure,” Erin said. “At this point, AptDeco has my furniture, I have no money, and I’m left chasing them for something I’m already owed. It’s an incredibly unsettling position to be in, particularly when so many other sellers seem to be experiencing the same thing. The fact that I continue to receive email marketing newsletters and see them selling via Google Ads—paying that platform before their sellers—is infuriating.”

After this article was published (and three days after we initially asked for comment), an AptDeco spokesperson gave 404 Media a convoluted explanation involving “bot swarms,” which it blamed for the delays in seller payouts. “Over the past few months, we’ve been dealing with an unprecedented volume of bot activity, some of it malicious. This has created a myriad of challenges that we’ve been actively working to address.These bot swarms, along with the broader cybersecurity challenges of an AI-evolving world, prompted us to significantly strengthen our site’s security to ensure the long-term protection of our buyers and sellers,” the spokesperson said. “To be clear, customer data has not been compromised in any way. However, we’ve been investing heavily in preventative measures to further protect our community. Unfortunately, some of these efforts have resulted in delays in seller payouts.  As you can imagine, cybersecurity is a complex and sensitive topic, making it challenging to communicate all the details broadly. That said, the issue has now been resolved, and outstanding payouts are being processed. Any seller with questions can email and will hear back within 1 business day. We appreciate your patience and understanding.”

When I asked for clarification because it was not clear how bot swarms would affect payouts, the spokesperson said “the bot swarm did not affect seller payouts.”

“We deployed code to further improve protections for our customers (given the bot swarms) which inadvertently impacted seller payout processing. Providing additional technical context would require a detailed understanding of our codebase and would likely be more information than is relevant or useful to readers,” they added. “That said, we sincerely apologize to our customers for the delays and are committed to making things right. The issue has been resolved, our security infrastructure remains extremely robust, and outstanding payouts are being processed. We appreciate you reaching out and giving us the opportunity to clarify. This will be our final comment on the matter.”

items.title: Black Neighborhoods Are Twice as Likely To House a Data Center, Study Finds
items.author: Matthew Gault
items.content:
Developers build data centers in communities of color at more than twice the rate they do in white neighborhoods, according to a new study from researchers at George Washington University and the Center for Security, Innovation & New Technology (CSINT) at American University.

According to the study, “Redlining in the Age of AI: The Relationship between Data Center Locations and Race in the US” majority-Black neighborhoods have 2.2 times the odds of hosting a data center than a white neighborhood in the same state. The number goes up to 2.6 in majority-Hispanic neighborhoods and 4.2 times in majority-Asian neighborhoods. “As the share of Black, Hispanic, and Asian residents in a neighborhood increases, so do the odds that the neighborhood hosts a data center,” the researchers wrote.

The researchers ran the numbers by examining 81,000 US census tracts and location data for 5,291 data centers. “We found that these racial disparities persist even after accounting for factors such as population, household income, education, land costs, proximity to major transmission lines, and state fixed effects,” they wrote. “These results hold even though data centers are concentrated in and around metropolitan areas, which are often more racially diverse.”

“We really wanted to look at this on a nationwide scale to see: is this something that fits into this broader structural racism story?” CSINT executive director Samantha Bradshaw told 404 Media. “What we did find was yes [...] neighborhoods that have data centers tend to have a higher ratio of people of color.”

Bradshaw and co-author Dhanaraj Thakur told 404 Media that they were inspired to do the study after reading stories about data centers in Memphis, Tennessee polluting Black and Brown communities. Another high profile case occurred in Taylor, Texas where a white family donated a tract of land to the city with the intention it become a public part. That land abutted a Black neighborhood. The city never built a park there and now it’s slated to become a data center

According to the researchers, the historical legacy of — the process of denying Americans of color loans and other opportunities to keep them in specific neighborhoods — is to blame for some of this. Data centers are often built near transmission lines because they provide ease of access to power infrastructure, for example. Those transmission lines were often built in majority Black neighborhoods in America. 

Thakur said he doubted that data centers developers were seeking to intentionally put data centers in communities of color. “It’s just how embedded race is with all these other factors,” he said. 

The study distinguished between several different kinds of data centers and noted there are massive differences between hyperscalers like what Meta, Google, and Grok are building and smaller mixed use buildings that often serve as network transmission hubs as well as compute warehouses, which the study called “co-location facilities.” When a hyperscaler comes to town, the developers sometimes promise economic investment in the community where it’s being constructed and those facilities typically aren’t built in communities of color..

Meta is building a $50 billion data center in rural Louisiana. Community leaders there have said it would bring 1,000 permanent jobs and that sales tax revenues have already jumped 2,000 percent, leading to a $50,000 bonus for area teachers. Even here, there is disparity. Most of the hyperscalers that promise massive economic benefits to local communities are built in white rural communities. 

The study makes several suggestions about what to do about all this including data center-specific zoning regulations, prioritizing racial equity in discussions around building them, and requiring racial impact statements for data centers before they’re built. 

Thakur and Bradshaw emphasized that tech policy should be a negotiation between the companies that provide the tech and the communities that use it. Data centers have spurred these conversations — they’re physical representations of Big Tech’s powers, a power that Americans recently rejected at the ballot box. “AI has a physical geography, and that geography is shaped by political and social history,” the researchers wrote in the study.

“I think the issue around how racial justice, civil rights plays into many other kinds of policies —health, education, housing, whatever it is — we just don't see enough of that consideration in tech policy, and I think this this kind of analysis shows why we should be doing that, thinking about that more,” Thakur said.

Bradshaw agreed. “If you look at who's represented in tech policy and who built these systems, who designs them, who engineers them, it's a very specific kind of white male Silicon Valley California ideology engineer, and that is not representative of the technology and its users,” she said. “So I think bringing in these perspectives is really really important because then we can truly think about ways to design a tech future that is for everybody.
